AN ACT OF WAR?
REPORTED CANTON SHIPPING RULES.
TREATIES VIOLATED?
Boycott
Shipping regulations which may amount to a declaration of war are reported to have been imposed by Canton, but whether they have official backing remains to be seen.
HITTING HONGKONG.
British
(Router's Service.)

The Chinese authorities have drawn "up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.
All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.
It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.
LOCAL COMMENT.

Opinions in Hongkong vary as to the outcome of the telegram. A gentleman who controls a fairly large number of ships vitally interested in trade with Canton pointed out to a “China” Mail” reporter that such a state of affairs had existed practically from the beginning of the “strike.”

"With the exception of ships under the Chinese flag," he said, "all vessels calling at Canton have been interfered with, even Chinese-owned shipping under foreign registry. Latterly Chinese steamers have discharged and loaded at Canton, but," so he believed, "only under payment of'squeeze' to strike officials who work hand in hand with administrative politicians. More recently some foreign tonnage had reached Canton, such as tramp and chartered ships with cargoes of rice from Bangkok, etc. Even food boats had to be'squared' before they could be cleared."

Continuing, the speaker said he took the message to mean that the so-called Canton Government had now actually come out in the open to sponsor the activities of the Strike Executive which was probably the “Anti-Imperialist Union” referred to in the cable. Certain shipping would continue to call at Canton, without coming to Hongkong but trade would suffer to an untold extent if British and Japanese hulls were prohibited.
CANTON MOVES.
Another gentleman, connected
TREACHERY TO CRUSH ENEMY.
HONAM BOUGHT OVER?

The “China Mail” learns from a reliable source that the Kuomintang Government is attempting to buy over General Li Fook-lam's troops before crushing him, so as to extend their power and remove opposition.

General Li has several thousand Cantonese troops who have been in Honam (the island opposite Canton) for some time. He is accused of refusing to obey the Bolshevik order to prohibit gambling and opium—from which are derived substantial revenues.

Recently General Li has moved his troops into surrounding villages for fear of being disarmed by the Reds and news has reached Hongkong that the Red leaders are aiming at "buying over" some of his detachments before challenging him to battle. At any rate, without support, Li would have been an easy prey for the Reds.

with river shipping, noted the fact that Hongkong would still be in communication with Canton if the order ever took effect, because there was nothing to prevent steamers running between Canton and Macao, and between Macao and Hongkong. This speaker expressed some very pronounced views. He said that the Kuomintang were imposing their will on the merchants regardless of whether foreign trade was crippled or not. In his opinion if the drafting of the rules could be legally brought to the door of the Kuomintang Government in Canton—and such could be done by obtaining the officially approved notices in all parts of the city—declaration of war was the only alternative. He was positive that by fouting trade treaties Canton rendered herself liable to war.
NEW P. & O. LINER.
S.S. NARKUNDA ARRIVES HERE.

The arrival in the harbour to-day of the s.s. Narkunda, the largest P. & O. liner to call at Hongkong, is of considerable interest, and the sight of her lying a short distance from the Empress boat with another three. funnel boat midstream is an imposing one.
The Narkunda carried the Earl and Countess of Reading as far as Bombay, also the new Commander in Chief of the forces in India,
VICEROY AS PASSENGER.
BIG P. & O. LINER.

Her calls here now and on the occasion of her return from Shanghai will be the only ones she is likely to make at Hong-kong for it is understood that upon her return to London the Narkunda will be transferred back to the London-Australia run for which she was originally built. On this temporary run Far Eastern prospective passengers are given the opportunity of observing this large and commodious liner which together with others on the Australian run will be available for connection to be made with them at Colombo.
The s.s. Narkunda which arrived here this morning.
DYNAMITE IN CAR.
CHINESE MOTHER AND SON. CONVICTED.
PRINCIPAL HEAVILY FINED.
The accused were travelling in a motor vehicle to Aberdeen and were found to be carrying 400 sticks of dynamite (the contents of a full case of δ0 lb.) and 400 detonators.
An old Chinese woman and her son were charged at the Central Magistracy this morning for an offence under the Dangerous Goods Ordinance.

The old woman, who was in the employment of the Tung.Wo Company, contractors, as stone-breaker, pleaded that she was engaged by her master to carry: the explosives to Aberdeen, where a man was to take delivery.
The Magistrate (Mr. McElderry) imposed a fine of $100 on each of the accensed, or two months' hard labour in default.

PRINCIPAL CHARGED.
Following the conviction, the muster of the Tung Wo firm of contractors, was charged on two counts of causing the two accused in the previous case to carry the explosives and with having a quantity of gunpowder in his matshed at Shubs Road without a permit.
Mr. L. D. Turner appeared for the defence.
STRIKE OVER.
Evidence, which was given at length, went to show that the exposures were removed without the knowledge of accused, who held a permit to carry dynamite for blasting purposes.
SHANGHAI POST OFFICE WORKERS RETURN

Mr. Turner submitted that there was no evidence to warrant conviction on the first charge. A plea of guilty was entered on the other charge of possession of gunpowder, which amounted to less than half a pound in weight.
His Worship convicted on both counts, a fine of $100 being imposed for possession of gunpowder and $600 on the more serious charge.

Foster smokers returned to work last night, agreeing to refer matters to Peking and or the promise that officials will recommend consideration of demands.

The vessel was built by Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., at Belfast, her keel being laid in 1920. Her length between uprights as 581.4 feet; her breadth 69.4 feet and moulded depth 40.75 feet. She is a vessel of 16,227 tons British register with a displacement of 22,000 tons on a normal draft of 27.7 feet. Fully laden her displacement is about 24,000 tons. Her cruising speed is about 18 knots. Her engineers which were also built by Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., are 18,000 h.p. and the diameter of her propellers 19ft. 3in. with a pitch of 23 feet.

The s.s. Narkunda which carries a crew of 457 is commanded by Captain H. G. Evans, R.N.B., the Commodore of the P. & O. Fleet, her Purser is Mr. C. Delmar-Cavendish and her Chief Engineer, Mr. A. B. Stuart. The vessel has accommodation for 444 first-class passengers, who are almost entirely berthed in single and two-berth cabins, and 247 2nd-class passengers berthed in single, two-berth, three-berth and four-berth cabins.
REMINDER FOR TO MORROW'S
10W TO JOIN.
DRIFT TO RUIN.
NEED FOR ACTION.

No reminder is needed concerning the meeting in connection with the re-establishment of a Hong Kong Branch of the China Association to be held at 5.15 p.m. sharp to-morrow at the board room of Messrs. Jardine Matheson & Co., Ltd.
HOME APATHY AND THE

Those desiring to join the Branch will be able to do so by signing the forms obtainable at the meeting and it is hoped especially in view of the present crisis in Hongkong and China that a very vigorous Branch will again spring into being.
MR. HOLYOAK'S LEAD.
The Home Government seeming not to have fully realized the gravity of the crisis out here, another public meeting has been called “to send a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.”
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—On Monday evening last at the meeting in the “Theatre Royal” I promised the audience that in the event of the reply from home being unfavourable to what was asked for, an opportunity would be given at an early date for the public to express its voice. A reply has come, it is confidential and therefor I am not at liberty to quote it, but it is quite evident that unless we can wake up the British Government to the urgent peril of the situation there is not a hope of armed intervention unless the “Powers” unite in action, and there is little probability of that, and so we are to wait the results of future Conference.
NO NOTICE.
PRINTERS' COOLIE WHO LEFT.
ALLEGED. CRIMPING.
A Chinese youth was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning by Mr. Labrum, of Ye Olde Printerie for leaving without notice.

The complainant stated that the accused was employed as a printer's coddle on a wage of $12 a month, and left without giving any notice. A few days later the accused was found to be in the employment of Messrs. Der A. Wing. Complainant added that he was losing his men owing to other printing establishments offering more than the usual standard of wages.

The accused claimed to be only an apprentice and ignorant of the law regarding one month's notice. He said he was obliged to leave owing to insufficient wages, and added that he was now receiving $24 a month.
A fine of $25 was imposed, of which $12 was to go to the complainant.
TYPHOON ABOUT.
MOVING NEAR SOUTH OF FORMOSA.
NO LOCAL WARNING.
A typhoon warning, received by the local American Consulate General at 1 p.m. to-day read:— Typhoon east of Southern Fortosa's direction unknown
When this edition went to Press no warning had been sent out by the Royal Observatory and no local signal had been hoisted.
DRIVERS CONVICTED.

A narrow escape was that of Mr. J. H. Simmons, Inspector of the Hongkong Tramway Company, according to the evidence given yesterday at the Central Magistracy against a taxi driver who was charged with negligent driving. As a result of the taxi running into his ricsha Mr. Simmons was thrown and the ricsha completely turned over. Ricsha puller and occupant both sustained minor injuries. In decision on the part of the taxi driver as to what direction to take was said to be the cause of the accident which occurred near the Tramway Shelter at Causeway Bay. Defendant was fined $10 and ordered to pay the ricsha coolie $10 compensation.
Peckless driving also formed one of the items in the list of breaches of Traffic Regulations brought against Chinese motor driver who was yesterday charged at the Kowloon Magistracy. The evidence showed that he drove round a band at Kwai

ences in the North, which in any case can never settle the Southern situation, or the report to the British Government of possibly some special Commissioner sent out from home, who, it may be, has not even been selected yet, to advise them of conditions out here, and meanwhile this Colony and British trade throughout Southern China drift daily nearer to utter ruin. Telegram upon telegram of the gravest possible nature has poured home from all sources, Government, public and private, stating the plain unvarnished truth: — manifestly they are either misunderstood or not believed—or else what is still more incredible nothing can be done.

The Theatre Royal has been booked for 5.15 next Tuesday, the 25th, and arrangements are in progress for a meeting at which the Colony will no doubt express its views in a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.

I trust the promoters may count on the united support of the "entire Press" here and all who are convinced of the vital necessity for prompt action in making the meeting as widely known and as successful as the extreme gravity of the situation demands. It cannot be too clearly stated again that it is apparently still not realised at home that this is no question of a "Strike" but of an organised and inspired attack upon British trade and interests in all our Treaty Ports and Concessions and upon this Colony in particular.

Yours, etc.,
P. H. HOLYOAK.
Hongkong, August 19, 1925.
SHANGHAI CONDITIONS.
DEFALCATION OF STRIKE
POSTAL OFFICIALS WAGES.
Shanghai. August 18.

A secret meeting of a number of unions affiliated to the general union of labour, education and commerce, have passed a resolution seceding from the latter. The action is due to the alleged defalcation of strike funds on the part of general union officials.
The situation on the waterfront is improving gradually: Wharf coolies mostly have resumed.

The Ministry of Communications at Peking has authorised the local post office officials to offer strikers an increase of wages, but the strikers have rejected it. Junior clerks starting at $20 a month were offered $35, but demand $52.50. The officials have requested the public not to use pillar boxes and to call at the post office for their mails.
